content: Japanese encephalitis (JE) is a severe viral infection that primarily affects the brain, causing inflammation known as encephalitis. This disease is prevalent in certain rural regions of Asia and is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. It is important to note that JE cannot be spread directly from one person to another. The clinical manifestations of Japanese encephalitis can range from mild to severe. Mild cases may present with fever and headache, while severe cases can lead to encephalitis, which is associated with a high mortality rate—approximately 25% of severe cases result in death. Symptoms of severe JE include headache, high fever, neck stiffness, stupor, disorientation, abnormal movements, occasional seizures (especially in infants), coma, and paralysis. To prevent Japanese encephalitis, it is essential to minimize exposure to mosquito bites. This can be achieved by staying in well-screened areas, wearing clothing that covers most of the body, and using effective insect repellents containing up to 30% N,N-diethyl-meta-toluamide (DEET) on the skin and clothing. Additionally, treating clothing with permethrin can further reduce the risk of mosquito bites. While the Japanese encephalitis vaccine is available and effective in preventing the disease, it is not 100% protective and should be used in conjunction with mosquito bite precautions. The JE vaccine is recommended for individuals who live in or travel to rural areas of Asia where the disease is endemic, as well as laboratory workers who may be exposed to the virus. The vaccination schedule consists of three doses: the second dose is administered seven days after the first, and the third dose is given 30 days after the first. The third dose should be completed at least 10 days before travel to ensure adequate protection and to allow time for medical care in case of delayed side effects. A booster dose may be required after two years. Children aged 1–3 years receive a smaller dose than older children and adults, and the vaccine is generally not recommended for children under one year of age. The JE vaccine can be administered alongside other vaccines. Certain individuals should not receive the JE vaccine. These include anyone who has experienced a life-threatening allergic reaction to mouse protein, thimerosal, or a previous dose of the JE vaccine. It is also important to inform your healthcare provider if you have severe allergies (e.g., hives or wheezing after a wasp sting or medications), are pregnant or breastfeeding, or will be traveling for fewer than 30 days, particularly if staying in urban areas where the risk of JE is lower. As with any vaccine, the JE vaccine can cause side effects, though the risk of serious harm or death is extremely low. Mild side effects include soreness, redness, or swelling at the injection site (affecting about 1 in 5 people), as well as fever, headache, muscle pain, abdominal pain, rash, chills, nausea/vomiting, or dizziness (affecting about 1 in 10 people). These symptoms typically occur shortly after vaccination and resolve within a few days. Moderate or severe reactions, such as serious allergic reactions (e.g., rash, swelling of the hands, feet, face, or lips, and difficulty breathing), have been reported. These reactions may occur within minutes to as long as 10–17 days after vaccination, with most occurring around 48 hours post-vaccination. Approximately 60 out of 10,000 vaccinated individuals experience allergic reactions. Rarely, severe problems such as seizures or nervous system issues have been reported, occurring in fewer than 1 in 50,000 vaccinated individuals. If a moderate or severe reaction occurs, it is important to monitor for unusual symptoms such as high fever, allergic reactions, or neurological problems within 1–30 days after vaccination. Signs of an allergic reaction may include difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, swelling of the extremities, face, or lips, paleness, weakness, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness. If any of these symptoms occur, seek medical attention immediately. Inform your healthcare provider about the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. You can also report the reaction to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) by calling 1-800-822-7967 or visiting their website. In rare cases of serious vaccine-related injury, the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) provides financial assistance for medical care. For more information about the VICP, call 1-800-338-2382 or visit their website. For additional information about the Japanese encephalitis vaccine, consult your healthcare provider, contact your local or state health department’s immunization program, or reach out to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) at 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visit the National Immunization Program’s website.
